Names in English (`fontNamesInEnglish`) only changes the UI menu labels, not this list. With `family` it gives that
family's styles (upright by weight, then italics) and fails when the family isn't available; `axes` lists a variable
font's variation axes (`tag`, `name`, `min`, `default`, `max`, `hidden`, and `value`, the setting of `style`, else of the
first style), empty for a static font. `text.rescanFonts`
(Character panel menu › Refresh Font List) scans the font folders again, for fonts installed or removed since the app
started: type set in a font that became available redraws in it, and type set in a family that was removed redraws in
the fallback font and is listed as missing, without editing the document. The app does so by
itself when its window comes to the front and a font folder changed meanwhile.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.fontList","params":{}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.fontList","params":{"family":"Source Serif 4"}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.rescanFonts","params":{}}}
```

`text.missingFonts` lists the fonts that the active document's type uses, in its layers and its symbols, and that aren't
available as named: `{fonts: [{family, style, status, resolved}], count, fontsNextToDocument?}`. `status` is `missing` or
`substitute`, as in `text.fonts`. CSS generic families such as `sans-serif`, which no font file provides, and names
longer than 256 bytes are left out. `fontsNextToDocument` is the `Fonts` folder next to the saved document
(File › Package writes it), when there is one and a search may start there. `text.findFontFiles {folder}` looks for
the fonts' files in an absolute folder and its subfolders on separate threads and returns at once with
`state: "searching"` and an `id`; `fonts: [{family, style?}]` names other fonts to look for. `text.findFontFiles {}`
returns the last search's state with the files found so far for each font: `searching`, `done`, `stopped` (with
`stopped`: `stop`, `time` or `limit`) or `failed` (with `error`); before the first search it returns
`{state: "idle", fonts: []}`, without an `id`. `{stop: true}` stops the search. A search reads the table directories
and the `name`, `fvar` and `OS/2` tables of `.ttf`, `.otf`, `.ttc` and `.otc` files and, on macOS, of suitcase fonts
(extensionless or `.suit` files whose fonts are in their resource fork), and it lists a file for a font only when adding
the file makes the font resolve exactly as `text.fonts` resolves it. It ends after `maxSeconds` (60 by default, 1 to
600), at its limits on the entries listed (10,000,000), the folders waiting to be listed (1,000,000), the font files
read (10,000) and the files kept (1,000), or once every font has a file. Folders more than 64 levels below the picked
one are skipped and counted in `skipped`. A search does not read a font file larger than 256 MB, which
`text.addFontFiles` does not copy, or a suitcase font whose resource fork is larger than 8 MB.

A search does not enter app and media library packages (`.app`, `.bundle`, `.framework`, `.photoslibrary` and the like),
folders named `Program Files` (also `Program Files (x86)` and `Program Files (Arm)`), `ProgramData`, `$Recycle.Bin` or
`System Volume Information`, the system's folders at the root of a volume (a macOS, Linux, BSD or Windows root, told by
the folders it holds), the `Shared` and `Public` folders in `Users`, a home folder's `Library`, `AppData`,
`Applications` and `snap` folders and the folders in it whose names start with a dot, the app data folders in a
`Library` folder (`Application Support`, `Containers`, `Group Containers`, `Caches`, `Preferences`), or the folders the
environment names for apps and the system (such as `APPDATA`, `LOCALAPPDATA`, `ProgramFiles`, `SystemRoot` and
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`), and a search of a folder inside one of them fails. The walk also skips other hidden folders and
folders whose contents are in the cloud, and it follows no links; a picked folder may be one of those, and a picked path
that goes through a link is searched at its target. Programs installed in other folders, such as a folder on another
drive, are searched as any other folder is.

`text.addFontFiles {files}` copies files that the session's last search found into VectorCraft's `Fonts` folder, then
scans the fonts again, and type set in them redraws. It copies only regular `.ttf`, `.otf`, `.ttc`, `.otc`, `.woff`
and `.woff2` files and suitcase fonts (with their resource fork), at most 256 MB a file and 1 GB in all, and lists any
other file in `skipped`. It never replaces a file: the names `Name.otf`, `Name 2.otf` up to `Name 99.otf` are tried in
turn until one is free, which gets the copy, or is a file with the same contents, which is kept (`kept`).
Copy only fonts you own or are licensed to install. `command.batch` returns before a search ends; later requests over MCP or the control channel poll
`text.findFontFiles {}`. `vectorcraft-cli run` stops the search when its last step ends. The web build has no Fonts
folder and no folder search.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.missingFonts","params":{}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.findFontFiles","params":{"folder":"/Users/me/Downloads"}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.findFontFiles","params":{}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.addFontFiles","params":{"files":["/Users/me/Downloads/Example/Example-Regular.otf"]}}}
```

## Tool options

`tool.setOption` reads and sets a tool's options, headless too: `{key, value}` or `{values: {…}}` sets them on the
active tool, `tool` names another one, and `{}` just reads them; the result is the tool's options. The options a
tool keeps last across tool switches (and documents) and are saved with the preferences (`toolSettings` in
`prefs.get`'s full object), as the reference app keeps them: the Liquify tools' brush and tool options, Mirror & Cut's
axis and side, Puppet Warp's mesh, the Symbolism brush, the line, grid, pencil, brush and eraser tools' options,
polygon sides and star points, the Flare Tool Options and the Shape Builder Tool Options. The Liquify tools share one set of Global Brush Dimensions (width, height, angle,
intensity), and the Symbolism tools one brush. Interaction state (pins, a reference point) starts afresh. In the
desktop app, while the Artboard tool is in use, a change to its `selected` or `active` makes the artboard it then has
active the active artboard (the navigator's and the Artboards panel's).

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"tool.setOption","params":{"tool":"twirl","values":{"width":60,"rate":90}}}}
```

`tool.options {tool}` opens what double-clicking the tool's button opens (its params doc lists every tool), in the
desktop app. The Flare tool's are its Flare Tool Options (dialog `flareOptions`): `diameter` and `pathLength` (pt),
`opacity`, `brightness`, `growth`, `fuzziness`, `longest`, `rayFuzziness` and `largest` (%), `rays`, `rings`,
`direction` (°), and `raysOn` and `ringsOn` (the Rays and Rings checkboxes; off, the flare has none). OK keeps them
(`tool.setOption {tool: "flare", values}`) and the next flare dragged out uses them; a click with the tool opens the
same dialog, and its OK also draws a flare there. The Artboard tool's are the active artboard's Artboard Options
(dialog `artboardOptions`; the Artboard tool's active artboard while it is in use, else the window's; its `x` and `y`
are the artboard's top-left corner in document points, while the dialog shows X and Y at the reference point the
Transform panel uses, counted from the ruler origin), a graph tool's
the selected graph's Graph Type (an error without one), a Symbolism tool's the Symbolism Tools Options (dialog
`symbolismOptions`: `diameter` in points, `intensity` and `density` 1–10, one brush for the eight tools) and the
Magic Wand tool's its panel. `ui.newArtboard` (Alt-click on the Artboards panel's New Artboard) opens Artboard Options
for a new artboard, with `new: true` and the name, position and size that `artboard.new {}` would give it. OK runs
`artboard.new` with the fields and makes the new artboard the active one, and Cancel adds no artboard.
`artboard.new` and `artboard.setProps` trim the white space around `name`, and a blank name gives the artboard its
default name, "Artboard N" for the Nth artboard.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"tool.setOption","params":{"tool":"flare","values":{"rays":24,"ringsOn":false}}}}
```

The Shape Builder tool's options are its Shape Builder Tool Options (dialog `shapeBuilderOptions`):
`openFilledAsClosed` (on: a filled open path bounds a region as if an invisible edge closed it; off: it cuts regions
as an unfilled path does), `pickColorFrom` (`artwork`, the default: a merged shape takes the appearance, opacity and
blending mode of the front-most selected object under the drag's first point, else of the one under its last point,
else of the front-most selected object; `swatches`: the current fill, and the Left and Right arrow keys step the
current fill through the document's color swatches), `cursorSwatchPreview` (off; with `swatches`, chips above the
pointer show the current fill and the swatches before and after it), `selection` (`freeform`, the default, or
`straightLine`: a drag touches what the line from its first point to the pointer crosses), `highlightFill` (on by
default; when it is off, merge mode shades no regions), `gapDetection` (off) with `gapLength` (pt, 0 to 72; 3), `clickStrokeSplitsPath` (In Merge Mode,
Clicking Stroke Splits the Path; off), `highlightStroke` (Highlight Stroke When Editable; on) and `highlightColor`
(`#rrggbb` or a layer color's name; `#ff4f4f`, the layer color Red). With `clickStrokeSplitsPath` on, in merge mode,
the pointer shows scissors within 4 screen pixels of a stroke, `highlightStroke` draws the run of stroke under it in
`highlightColor`, and a click splits that run off its path: the run goes from the anchor or crossing point before the
pointer to the one after it, the path keeps the rest of it, and a copy of the path with the run, in the path's
direction, goes directly above it. Both keep the path's gradients where they were on it.
A lone rectangle's side is such a run. A lone line is a run that is all of its path, and a run that would leave 0.05 pt
or less of its path (a ten-thousandth of the larger side of a path over 500 pt) counts as all of it, so the pointer
shows no scissors over it and a click on it does not split it. A release up to 3 screen pixels from the press is a
click when the pointer went no farther during the drag.
With `pickColorFrom` `swatches`, the run takes the current fill as its stroke. The tool sends `openFilledAsClosed`,
`pickColorFrom`, the gap length (`gap`, 0 with Gap Detection off) and, for such a click, `splitStroke: true` with
`shapeBuilder.merge`, which takes them all as params, and `shapeBuilder.regions` takes `openFilledAsClosed` and `gap`.
`shapeBuilder.merge` with `splitStroke` returns the run's id as `split`.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"tool.setOption","params":{"tool":"shapeBuilder","values":{"selection":"straightLine","pickColorFrom":"swatches"}}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"shapeBuilder.merge","params":{"points":[[50,-1]],"splitStroke":true}}}
```

With Shift held at the press, a Shape Builder drag draws a rectangular marquee from where the drag started to the
pointer, and the Selection option does not apply to it. The regions the marquee reaches are shaded while it is drawn
and merge into one shape on release; with Alt also held at the press, they are deleted. The marquee reaches a region
when the region's outline crosses the rectangle or has an anchor inside it, or when the region holds the whole
rectangle. The tool sends the marquee to `shapeBuilder.merge` as `rect: [x, y, width, height]` in place of `points`:
`x` and `y` are where the drag started, and the width and height are negative for a drag up or to the left. For Pick
Color From Artwork, the corner where the drag started counts as the drag's first point, and the opposite corner counts
as its last: the merged shape takes the look of the front-most selected object under the first corner, else of the one
under the opposite corner, else of the front-most selected object. A Shift-click that does not move sends `points`
as a click does, so with `clickStrokeSplitsPath` on, a Shift-click on a stroke splits it. A marquee splits no stroke,
however little the pointer moves: the tool sends no `splitStroke` with `rect`, and `shapeBuilder.merge` does not split
a stroke when it has `rect`. With both `rect` and `points`, the command also touches what the points touch.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"shapeBuilder.merge","params":{"rect":[50,50,200,200]}}}
```

## Perspective grid

The grid is document data (`perspective.grid.set` edits the model directly). `perspective.grid.get` reads it:
`grid` (the model), `define` (the Define Grid fields), `station` (the viewer: `x` the centre of vision on the
horizon `y`, `distance` from the picture plane, in points) and `defined` (false while the document uses the default
grid). `perspective.grid.define` sets the grid from the Define Grid fields: `kind`, `units`, `scale`
(`[artboard, real world]`), `gridline`, `angle` (the viewing angle, 0–90°), `distance` (the viewing distance),
`horizonHeight`, `thirdVp` (`[x right, y up]` from the centre of vision), `leftColor`, `rightColor`, `groundColor`
(`"#rrggbb"`) and `opacity` (0–100). Lengths are real-world lengths in `units` drawn at `scale`; missing fields keep the
grid's. Only what differs changes (an unchanged OK is no undo step): a new type, angle or distance moves the vanishing
points around the station point, which stays put. In two- and three-point grids the viewer looks at the left plane at
the viewing angle, so the vanishing points sit at `x − distance/tan(angle)` and `x + distance·tan(angle)`.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.grid.get","params":{}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.grid.define","params":{"units":"inches","gridline":0.5,"angle":30,"distance":6,"horizonHeight":3}}}
```

Perspective grid presets: `perspective.presets.list` lists the built-in views (`[1P-Normal View]`, `[1P-Low View]`,
`[1P-High View]`, `[2P-Normal View]`, `[2P-Low View]`, `[2P-High View]`, `[3P-Normal View]`, `[3P-Low View]`;
`builtIn: true`, fitted to the first artboard, protected), then the saved ones, each with its Define Grid fields.
`perspective.grid.preset {name}` (or `{kind}`, that type's normal view) resets the grid to one, fitted to the first
artboard. `perspective.presets.save {name?, newName?, preset?, …fields}` saves a preset: just `{name}` saves the
document's grid (View → Perspective Grid → Save Grid as Preset). `perspective.presets.delete {name}`,
`perspective.presets.export {names?, path?}` (a `.vcperspective` JSON file; without `path` it returns `data`) and
`perspective.presets.import {path? | data? | dataBase64?, replace?}` manage them. Saved presets are kept with the
preferences, and a grid whose fields are a preset's is named after it (`name`).

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.grid.preset","params":{"name":"[2P-Low View]"}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.presets.save","params":{"name":"Street","units":"feet","scale":[1,48],"gridline":1}}}
```

Perspective grid view options (View → Perspective Grid; view state saved with the document, no undo step, each
`{on?: bool}`, no param toggles, → `{on}`): `perspective.grid.lock` (Lock Grid: the grid's widgets can't be dragged),
`perspective.grid.lockStation` (Lock Station Point: dragging one vanishing point turns the view around the station
point, so the other one moves), `perspective.grid.snap` (Snap to Grid, on by default: `perspective.draw` lands the
drawn corners, and `perspective.move` the nearer edge, on gridlines within a quarter cell; both take `snap: false`)
and `perspective.grid.rulers` (Show Rulers: a ruler up the line where the planes meet, in the grid's units at its
scale). Gridlines draw in the Define Grid colours at its opacity.

Perspective grid widgets: with the Perspective Grid tool (`pointer_gesture`), the vanishing points (Shift keeps the
horizon; with Lock Station Point the other one swings), the horizon, the third vanishing point, the origin, the left
and right ground-level points (24 px from the origin along each wall's ground line: they move the whole grid; Shift
keeps one axis), the left and right extents (separate: `extent` and `extentRight`; Alt drags both, Shift goes by
whole cells), the vertical extent and the cell size widget (on the line where the planes meet, a cell up, or more
cells while they're small) reshape the grid; Lock Grid stops them. The Plane Switching Widget stays put in a corner
of the document window (headless: the first artboard's top-left corner); a press on it picks the plane with any tool
while the grid shows (choosing a perspective tool shows it, and `perspective.grid.show` hides it again with the tool
still chosen), and the keys 1–4 (`key` with `"1"`…`"4"`) pick the left, horizontal, right and no plane.
`perspective.widget.options {show?, position?}` (Perspective Grid Options, double-click the tool) hides it or moves
it to `topLeft`, `topRight`, `bottomLeft` or `bottomRight`, kept with the preferences (`prefs.get`/`prefs.set` key
`perspectiveWidget`).

## Envelopes

Object → Envelope Distort wraps the selection in a live envelope: `object.envelope.makeWithWarp` (`style`: arc,
arcLower, arcUpper, arch, bulge, shellLower, shellUpper, flag, wave, fish, rise, fisheye, inflate, squeeze or twist;
`bend`, `h` and `v` in % from -100 to 100; `horizontal` or `orientation`), `object.envelope.makeWithMesh` (`rows`,
`cols`: 1–50) and `object.envelope.makeWithTopObject` (the topmost selected path becomes the envelope).
`object.envelope.info` reads the selected envelope's settings (`type`, the warp's or mesh's values, `fidelity` and
the options, `editing`), or with no envelope selected the options new envelopes get. With an envelope selected,
`object.envelope.resetWithWarp` and `object.envelope.resetWithMesh` (`rows`, `cols`, `maintainShape`: true keeps
the current shape) switch its kind and keep its content. `object.envelope.options` sets `fidelity` and the options
(`antiAlias`, `preserveShape`: clippingMask or transparency, `distortAppearance`, `distortLinearGradients`,
`distortPatternFills`; the last two need `distortAppearance`); with no envelope selected it sets them for new
envelopes. New envelopes start with Distort Appearance on, as in the reference app; envelopes saved before these
options existed keep their old look (appearance applied after the distortion).

`object.envelope.release` gives back the content and the envelope's shape (a grey gradient mesh for warp and mesh
envelopes, the path for a top-object envelope); the content keeps the envelope's opacity, blend mode and opacity mask
(a group around it carries them when there are several objects). `object.envelope.expand`, and `object.expand` with
`object` on, replace envelopes by groups of their distorted content that keep the name, transparency, knockout and
opacity mask.
Type inside an envelope distorts as its glyph outlines, run by run in each run's paint, on the canvas and in every
export (SVG, PDF, EPS, EMF/WMF, DXF).
Everything inside bends with the envelope: images as a raster mesh warp (cut into pieces by Fidelity, each a clipped
image under its own affine map; SVG shares the pixels between the pieces), symbol instances as their symbol's art,
and with Distort Appearance strokes (as their filled outlines) and geometry effects; with it, Distort Linear Gradients
bends linear gradients and Distort Pattern Fills the pattern tiles. A transformed envelope keeps its warp in its own
frame (`kind.frame` in `document.inspect`; rotating a warp envelope turns the warp with it), and move and scale keep
it square to the page.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.envelope.makeWithWarp","params":{"style":"arch","bend":40}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.envelope.resetWithMesh","params":{"rows":3,"cols":3,"maintainShape":true}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.envelope.options","params":{"fidelity":80,"distortAppearance":true,"distortLinearGradients":true}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.envelope.info","params":{}}}
```

## Liquify tools

The Liquify tools (`warp`, `twirl`, `pucker`, `bloat`, `scallop`, `crystallize`, `wrinkle`) drag a brush over paths:
the selected ones, or with nothing selected every path the brush passes over. A stroke is one undo step and one
`object.liquify` journal entry, which an agent can also run directly. Their options (`tool.setOption`) are the Global
Brush Dimensions shared by the seven tools (`width`, `height` in pt, `angle`, `intensity` 0..1, `usePressure`,
`showBrush`) and the tool's own: `detail` (1..10); `simplify` (0..100) with `simplifyOn` (Warp, Twirl, Pucker,
Bloat); `rate` (Twirl, -180..180°); `complexity` (0..15) and `affectAnchors`, `affectIn`, `affectOut` (Scallop,
Crystallize, Wrinkle: what the brush moves); `horizontal`, `vertical` (Wrinkle, 0..1). Alt-drag sizes the brush from
its current size (with Shift too it keeps its proportions). With Use Pressure Pen on, each `pointer_gesture` event's
`pressure` (0..1) is the intensity there, and `object.liquify` takes points as `[x, y, pressure]`.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"tool.setOption","params":{"tool":"bloat","values":{"width":80,"height":80,"usePressure":true}}}}
{"name":"pointer_gesture","arguments":{"tool":"bloat","events":[{"kind":"down","x":280,"y":150,"pressure":0.3},{"kind":"drag","x":280,"y":200,"pressure":0.8},{"kind":"up","x":280,"y":250}]}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.liquify","params":{"tool":"scallop","points":[[300,150],[300,250]],"complexity":3,"affectAnchors":false}}}
```

Holding the brush still keeps Twirl, Pucker and Bloat working, scaled by the time held: every tenth of a second the
stroke's last point repeats in `object.liquify`'s `points`, one more dab there (other tools ignore repeated points).
Give a `pointer_gesture` event `holdMs` (0..60000) to hold the pointer that long after it, button down; the same
time gives the same result. Liquify reshapes paths only: type, symbols, images, graphs, meshes, and envelopes,
repeats and blends with their contents stay as they are, and guides are never touched. `object.liquify` returns
those under the brush in `skipped` with a `warning`, which the gesture's `requests` carry as `{"status": …}` (the
status bar in the app). A drag applies only the dabs each new sample adds; the result equals applying the whole
stroke at once, so the journal entry replays it exactly.

```json
{"name":"pointer_gesture","arguments":{"tool":"twirl","events":[{"kind":"down","x":300,"y":200,"holdMs":800},{"kind":"up","x":300,"y":200}]}}
```

The Liquify, Puppet Warp and perspective commands refuse a string or another value that is not a number with
`` `diameter` must be a number, not "40" ``, naming the key, and leave the document and its undo history as they
were: `diameter`, `width`, `height`, `angle`, `intensity`, `detail`, `simplify`, `rate`, `complexity`, `horizontal`
and `vertical` in `object.liquify`, with any `tool`; `expand` in `object.puppetWarp` and `object.puppetWarp.pins`;
`depth` in `perspective.transform`; `dx` and `dy` in `perspective.nudge`; and `offset` and `by` in
`perspective.plane.move`. A null is read as a key left out. `object.puppetWarp` refuses an `angles` entry that is not
a number or null with "angles must be a list as long as pins (degrees or null)", `perspective.draw` refuses an `at`
that is not two numbers, such as `["450", 380]`, with "`at` must be [x, y]", and `stroke.widthProfile.set` refuses a
point that is not three numbers, such as `[0.5, "1", 2, 2]`, with "points must be [t, left, right] with non-negative
widths".

## Perspective Selection

Objects in perspective keep their attachment themselves (`perspective` on the object: `plane` and `depth`, the
distance along the plane's normal), so copies, duplicates and pastes stay attached. With the
`perspectiveSelection` tool, a drag moves the selection within its plane (`perspective.move`; Alt copies), the
bounding-box handles scale it in plane space (`perspective.transform`; Shift keeps proportions, Alt scales about the
centre), and `press_key` `5` during a drag switches the move to perpendicular to the plane (press again to switch
back). The arrow keys nudge a selection in perspective by the keyboard increment (`perspective.nudge`; Shift ×10, Alt
copies). Object › Transform › Transform Again repeats the last perspective move or scale in plane space.

```json
{"name":"pointer_gesture","arguments":{"tool":"perspectiveSelection","events":[{"kind":"down","x":480,"y":410},{"kind":"drag","x":470,"y":405}]}}
{"name":"press_key","arguments":{"key":"5"}}
{"name":"pointer_gesture","arguments":{"events":[{"kind":"up","x":470,"y":405}]}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.transform","params":{"matrix":[1.5,0,0,1.5,0,0],"copy":true}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.transformAgain","params":{}}}
```

The perspective, width point, Liquify and Puppet Warp commands refuse a string, a number or another value that is not
true or false with `` `copy` must be true or false ``, naming the key, and leave the document and its undo history as
they were: `copy`, `perpendicular` and `snap` in `perspective.move`; `copy` in `perspective.transform`; `big` and
`copy` in `perspective.nudge`; `snap` in `perspective.draw`; `reproject` in `perspective.grid.set`; `visible` in
`perspective.grid.show`; `adjustAdjoining` in `stroke.widthPoint.set`; `usePressure`, `simplifyOn`, `affectAnchors`,
`affectIn` and `affectOut` in `object.liquify`, with any `tool`; and `rest` in `object.puppetWarp`. A null is read as
a key left out.

Planes move along their normals: `perspective.plane.move {plane, offset | by, objects}` (`leftOffset`,
`rightOffset`, `groundOffset` in the grid). The plane widgets (a diamond on each plane, drawn while the grid shows)
do it with the Perspective Grid and Perspective Selection tools: a plain drag moves the plane alone, Shift-drag moves
the objects on it too, Alt-drag copies them; double-clicking a widget (or `ui.perspectivePlane {plane}`) opens the
`perspectivePlane` dialog (`location` in points, `objects`: none, move or copy). Objects keep their place when the
grid's definition changes, as in the reference app; `perspective.grid.set` with `reproject: true` moves them with it
instead. `perspective.plane.matchObject` (Object › Perspective › Move Plane to Match Object) moves the plane of the
selected object onto it.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.plane.move","params":{"plane":"right","offset":40,"objects":"move"}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.plane.matchObject","params":{}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"ui.perspectivePlane","params":{"plane":"ground"}}}
```

Type and symbol instances attached to a plane stay type and symbol instances: their `perspective` record keeps a
`projection` (a 3 × 3 matrix) the canvas and every export (SVG, PDF, EPS, EMF/WMF, DXF, PNG) draw their outlines
through, so they are really foreshortened and still editable. `perspective.editText` (Object › Perspective › Edit
Text, or double-clicking the type with the Perspective Selection tool) shows the type flat where it is drawn, in
isolation mode, for the Type tool and `text.*` commands; `object.exitIsolation` projects it again. Release with
Perspective keeps their look. Shape, spiral, polar grid and flare drags draw on the active plane while the grid
shows, and so do the click-to-size dialogs (`perspective.draw` with `at`: the click; sizes are plane units).

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.editText","params":{}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.setText","params":{"text":"OPEN"}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.exitIsolation","params":{}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"perspective.draw","params":{"command":"shape.rectangle","params":{"x":470,"y":300,"width":50,"height":30},"at":[470,300]}}}
```

## Blends

`object.blend.make` blends the selected objects (or `ids`) into a live blend. Spacing and orientation default to
what `object.blend.options` set with no blend selected (`object.blend.info` reads them: `target: "defaults"`),
else Smooth Color and Align to Page. `starts` gives, per object, the anchor of its first subpath the blend starts
from (as the Blend tool's clicks on anchor points do; an open path's last anchor runs it the other way). A blend
among the objects takes the others in as more key objects, keeping its options, name and transparency:

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.blend.make","params":{"ids":[12,15],"starts":[0,2],"steps":8}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.blend.make","params":{"ids":[20,31]}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.blend.info","params":{}}}
```

A blend's spine is the straight lines between its key centres until it is edited. `object.blend.info` lists it
(`spine.anchors`, `keyAnchors`: the point each key sits on). `object.blend.spine.addAnchor {x, y}` adds a point where
the spine passes nearest, `object.blend.spine.moveAnchor {anchor, x, y}` moves a point (a key on it moves along; with
`handle: "in" | "out"` it places that handle), `object.blend.spine.convertAnchor {anchor, to: "smooth" | "corner", x?, y?}` converts a point's handles (a Smooth drag with `x, y` creates opposite handles; Corner retracts both), `object.blend.spine.reshapeSegment {segment, t, dx, dy, perpendicular?}` bends a segment
so its point at `t` moves by (dx, dy), turning a straight spine into a curve (`perpendicular` works as in `path.reshapeSegment`), and `object.blend.spine.removeAnchor
{anchor}` deletes a point no key sits on; the first edit turns the spine into a path. Moving a key moves its end of the spine. Release
(`object.blend.release`) leaves the spine as a path that paints nothing (`spines` in the result):

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.blend.spine.addAnchor","params":{"id":40,"x":150,"y":100}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.blend.spine.moveAnchor","params":{"id":40,"anchor":1,"x":150,"y":20}}}
```

How blends interpolate: closed shapes start where they twist least unless `starts` picks the anchors; strokes
interpolate weight, dashes (a solid stroke counts as the dashed one with its gaps closed), miter limit, arrowhead scale
and width profiles, while caps, joins, alignment, arrowheads and brushes switch halfway; gradients of one kind with
different stop counts resample to a common set of stops. Groups pair their members in stacking order (members only
one group has grow out of the other's centre), compound paths stay compound paths, and type, symbol instances and
images interpolate their transforms (type also its colours, stroke weight and size run by run; the words and the
symbol switch halfway). New blends are knockout groups (`object.setProps {knockout}` changes it), drawn on the
canvas as they export. `object.blend.expand` and `object.blend.release` keep the blend's name, transparency,
opacity mask and appearance (Release on a group around the keys and spine when the blend has any), and
`object.expand` with `object: true` expands the blends in the selection.

## Objects on Path

`object.objectsOnPath.attach {path?, ids?, pivot?, rotate?}` attaches the selected objects (or `ids`) to the path
`path`: the objects and the path go into an Objects on Path group, with the path at its bottom. The objects go along
the path in their order on the canvas, column by column from left to right and top to bottom in each column. The first
one sits on the path's first anchor, the last one sits on the end of an open path, and the others are spread evenly
between them by length; on a closed path the gaps run all the way round. The attachment point of each object (`pivot`,
0 to 8 row by row from the top left of its bounds without strokes; default 4, the center) sits on the path, and the
object is turned to the path's direction there. An object rotated by other than a multiple of 90° is first turned to
the nearest multiple. `rotate` tilts every object by that many degrees counter-clockwise. Without `path`, the command
chooses the Objects on Path tool (`objectsOnPath`), whose click on a path sends `{path}`. As the path, the command
refuses a guide, a compound path, type, a path without length, a path already in an Objects on Path group, a
clipping path, and a path inside a compound path, blend, envelope, repeat or Intertwine group. As objects, it skips
layers and refuses graphs, objects already in an Objects on Path group, clipping paths, and objects inside a blend,
envelope, repeat or Intertwine group; a member of a compound path attaches as its whole compound path. The tool
does not highlight a clipping path or a path inside a blend, envelope, repeat or Intertwine group, and a click on one
attaches nothing.

The group stays live: after every edit its objects go back on its path. Editing the path moves them, an object moved
on its own goes back to its place, an object moved into the group (`layer.move` with `place: "inside"`) joins the end
of the path, an object moved out of it leaves, and art that replaces an object (`symbol.breakLink`) keeps its place.
`object.objectsOnPath.options {ids?, pivot?, rotate?}` changes Pivot and Rotate, and
`object.objectsOnPath.expand {ids?}` makes the groups plain groups. Both act on the groups that `ids` names (Objects
on Path groups or objects in them), or on the groups of the selection when `ids` is not given. The native file keeps
the group with an `objects_on_path` record; SVG, PDF and the other exports write the path and the objects as plain
art.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.objectsOnPath.attach","params":{"path":30,"ids":[12,15,18]}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.objectsOnPath.options","params":{"pivot":7,"rotate":15}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.objectsOnPath.expand","params":{}}}
```

## Paragraph composer

`text.setFormat {ids?, composer: "singleLine"|"everyLine"}` sets how a text object's lines are broken (the Paragraph
panel menu's Single-line and Every-line Composer; stored in the paragraph attributes as `para.composer`, saved only
when it is Single-line). Every-line, the default, picks the breaks of the whole paragraph together in area type:
justified text gets even word spacing, ragged text (left, centre or right aligned) an even rag, so it may move a word
that fits to the next line to avoid a lone short word on the last line or a full line next to a short one.
Single-line fills each line as far as it goes. Point type and type on a path have no line width, so both composers
give the same result there. A paragraph whose characters differ in line metrics (type size, font, leading or vertical
scale, or an inline graphic taller than the text) is composed with Every-line in rectangular area type, rows and
columns included; in area type of another shape, or with text wrap, it falls back to Single-line.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"text.setFormat","params":{"ids":[7],"composer":"singleLine"}}}
```

## Editing envelopes

`object.envelope.editContents {editing}` switches between editing the envelope and its contents (the menu item reads
Edit Envelope while the contents are edited; it has no default shortcut, since the reference app's is Paste in Place
here). While the contents are edited, clicks hit the content where it sits undistorted and the Selection tool selects
it. A mesh envelope's points have bezier handles (`kind.handles`, offsets
right/left/down/up; none stored means the smooth mesh through the points, as older files have):
`object.envelope.setMeshPoint {id, index, x, y, handle?}` and `object.mesh.movePoint`, `object.mesh.addLine` and
`object.mesh.deletePoint` edit them like a gradient mesh's (one undo step each). On the canvas a selected envelope
shows its mesh; the Mesh tool and Direct Selection drag its points and the clicked point's handles, and the Mesh tool
adds a row and a column where it clicks inside. The Control bar shows Edit Envelope / Edit Contents, the warp's
style, orientation, bend and distortions (or the mesh's rows and columns), Reset (an unbent warp, a flat mesh) and
Envelope Options.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.envelope.editContents","params":{"editing":true}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"object.mesh.movePoint","params":{"id":12,"index":4,"x":220,"y":140,"handle":0}}}
```

## Shortcut sets from other apps

`shortcutSet.read {path? | data? | dataBase64?, name?}` reads a shortcut set another app saved as text (a `.kys` file
that starts with `/Menus {`) without changing the document or the preferences. Each block that sets `/Key` is an
entry, listed with its `name`, its `section` (the names of the blocks around it), its codes as the file writes them
(`key`, `modifiers`, `context`, `represent`) and its `line`. `codes` counts the entries that use each key and modifier
code, and `unread` lists the tokens the reader skipped, with their lines. The reader stops at 4 MiB, 16 open blocks,
20,000 entries and 8 MiB of names over the entries and their sections, cuts names at 1,024 bytes, and sets `truncated` when it reaches one of these limits. An XML shortcut
file fails with "This shortcut file is in a form VectorCraft can't read."

The import matches record what the names and codes in such files stand for in VectorCraft. They are kept with the
preferences, and resetting the preferences keeps them. `importMatches.set {matches: [{kind, name, target, label?}]}`
records them: kind `name` maps an entry name to a command id, `tool:<id>` or `panel:<id>`, and kinds `key` and
`modifiers` map a code, written in decimal, to a key or to modifiers as Edit › Keyboard Shortcuts writes them (`K`,
`Cmd+Shift`). A `target` of `""` records that there is no equivalent (for kind `modifiers`, no modifiers), and `null`
removes the match. `importMatches.list {kind?, query?}` lists them and `importMatches.reset {kind?}` removes them.
`shortcutSet.read` then adds the saved `target` to each entry, a `chord` to each entry whose codes are both known, and
the saved `key` or `mods` to each code.

In the desktop app, Edit › Keyboard Shortcuts › Import… and File › Open show such a file in Import Shortcut Set
(`ui.shortcutImportDialog {path? | dataBase64?, name?}` over the control channel). The dialog proposes targets from
the entry names and decodes the codes that VectorCraft's default shortcuts agree on.

```json
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"shortcutSet.read","params":{"path":"/Users/me/Studio.kys"}}}
{"name":"run_command","arguments":{"command":"importMatches.set","params":{"matches":[{"kind":"name","name":"Group","target":"object.group"},{"kind":"key","name":"901","target":"G"}]}}}
```

### PDF backend

# PDF backend

PDF writing uses `craft-pdf` from `storytold/craft-libs`, pinned to
`a0916808f7d78bed8c7b90cdf937176015454a7f`. Its `write` feature supplies Krilla configuration,
metadata construction, fallible font preparation and serialization, and native unwind guards.
The dependency disables default features and enables `write` and `interpret`.
The production writer retains Krilla’s raster-image support without its optional text shaper.
PDF test fixtures enable `simple-text` through a dev dependency.
The PDF crate explicitly retains the `flate2` `zlib-rs` feature previously supplied
by the registry reader, preserving compressed export bytes and their derived document IDs.

VectorCraft owns document traversal, drawing, font selection and embedding policy, colour
conversion, presets, page boxes, layers, editing data, postprocessing and print composition.
Editable import keeps its VectorCraft adapter, layer routing, colour policy and text decisions.
Desktop printer submission remains in `craft-print`.

The shared writer vendors Krilla 0.8.2 with an unwind-safe cleanup and poisoning patch.
The root `[patch.crates-io]` selects that copy from the same immutable revision: Cargo does
not inherit a dependency workspace's patches. A failed page or surface cleanup poisons the
backend document, so serialization cannot return an incomplete PDF after unwinding.
The shared crate's compile-time backend marker and `cargo xtask pdf-deps` (included in CI)
check that the patched writer is used. Krilla retains its MIT OR Apache-2.0 licensing;
its upstream provenance and authored patch are recorded in the shared repository.

Export and print construction, drawing and postprocessing run inside the shared native
unwind guard. These guards do not catch WASM aborts or process-wide allocation failures.
VectorCraft retains its finite-coordinate checks and the existing behavior that omits art
outside the writer's supported coordinate range. Font preparation checks the shared
512 MiB per-font copy limit and variation coordinates before allocation; failure preserves
VectorCraft's reported outline fallback. The writer is not a peak-memory or runtime budget.

PDF reading uses the same shared revision's patched Hayro syntax 0.7.2, interpreter 0.7.0
and JBIG2 0.3.0. This snapshot also retains CCITT 0.3.0 and JPEG 2000 0.3.5.
Its established Lab conversion uses Bradford adaptation; calibrated gray/RGB and tint-function
conversion retain floating-point precision. This policy differs from the registry 0.8 reader's
Lab profile and byte-quantized conversion and is assessed against independent colour expectations.
The application explicitly preserves its existing accepted file sizes with
`OpenOptions { max_input_bytes: usize::MAX, ..Default::default() }`; this migration adds no
new file-size ceiling. Ordinary decoded streams use the shared backend's immutable
per-document limits. Those limits are separate from streaming page-content budgets and
do not bound aggregate document or process memory. Password classification and the
existing permissions-password fallback remain application policy.

The layer and overprint pre-scan consumes `ContentReader` windows through `TypedIter`,
retaining graphics and marked-content state between windows. It does not collect a whole
page before scanning. Reaching the scan's operator, nesting or instruction-window limit,
a reported failed/truncated stream, a cap-reaching filtered form, or an undecidable final
operand tail returns an import error and discards the partial document. Previously the
operator limit could return a partial layer routing with a warning. Interpreter completion
warnings also become errors before a document is returned. Whitespace and comments at
EOF remain valid. The typed iterator does not classify every malformed operator, so this
is known-incomplete rejection rather than a general PDF validity certificate.

The five patched Hayro crates and Krilla are selected in the root `[patch.crates-io]`
from the same immutable revision as `craft-pdf`. `cargo xtask pdf-deps` rejects missing,
duplicate, local-path, registry and mismatched revisions for those seven packages.
`craft-print`, `craft-ui` and the other craft-libs crates use the same revision.

Dependency asset hashes and sources are in `ASSETS.md`; redistributed license texts are
in `licenses/pdf-backend`. Package staging carries those texts together with `NOTICE`
and `ASSETS.md`. Fonts and profiles remain dependency data; this repository adds no font
or profile binaries. Native page interpretation has a shared unwind guard; WASM aborts
and process-wide allocation failures cannot be caught.

The shared parser retains current main's 64-level cap for direct arrays and dictionaries,
including decoded content and object streams. The application retains its two-pass traversal
of repaired object tables, 16-link function/colour-space cap, 64-level calculator-procedure cap,
256 MiB stream checks and predictor validation. Native interpretation uses the existing
16 MiB stack wrapper, and imported document depth remains bounded.

Known incomplete decoded content remains an import error, including deeply nested operands
that the bounded parser cannot finish. Lowered ordinary decode limits and dictionary delimiters
split across scan windows are covered by synthetic regressions; they require the typed
incomplete-content error and never return a partial document. The former 256-level lexical
preflight and its diagnostic are superseded by the parser cap and completion checks.
The scratch bound does not cover whole-filter fallback decoding or aggregate parser/process memory.

### Plug-ins: the WebAssembly plug-in API (ABI v1)

# Plug-ins: the WebAssembly plug-in API (ABI v1)

VectorCraft does not host native plug-ins built for other illustration apps: that needs unsafe FFI into
arbitrary machine code and cannot work in the browser build. Instead, plug-ins are **WebAssembly modules**
run in a sandbox. One `.wasm` file works on macOS, Windows, Linux and the web. The design follows PhotoCraft's
plug-in API (same sandbox, same manifest and parameter schema), extended for vector documents.

There are three kinds of plug-in:

- **Object filters** read the selected paths and compound paths (geometry, fills, strokes, gradients, opacity)
  and return the objects to keep, change or add. A run is one undo step. Use them for recolouring, path
  clean-up, halftones, generative patterns and the like.
- **Live effects** rewrite one object's geometry each time it is drawn, from its appearance stack, like the
  built-in Distort & Transform effects. The art stays editable: move or reshape it and the effect follows.
- **Exporters** write the whole document in a file format of their own, for pen plotters, cutting machines,
  laser cutters and the like. File › Export › Export As lists them after the built-in formats, and the host writes the
  bytes they return: a plug-in still never touches a file.

This page is the contract for plug-in authors and the reference for the host (`crates/plugins`, the
`plugin.*` commands in `crates/engine/src/cmd/plugin.rs`).

## Using plug-ins

| Command | Params | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `plugin.list` | `{}` | `{"plugins": [{id, name, version, kind, author, description, params, paramsSchema, effect?, format?, extensions?, budget?, size, source}], "folder": report}` (`budget: "heavy"` for a [heavy filter](#heavy-filters)) |
| `plugin.info` | `{"id"}` | One plug-in: the `plugin.list` entry plus `manifest`, `defaults` and `lastError` (a live effect's last failure). |
| `plugin.run` | `{"id", "params"?: {…}, "ids"?: [...]}` (plug-in params may also be top-level keys) | Runs an object filter on the selection (or `ids`). One undo step; the result is selected. |
| `plugin.install` | `{"path": "/x/y.wasm"}` (desktop) or `{"dataBase64": "…", "name"?}`, `"replace": bool = true`, `"allowHeavy": bool = false` | Validates and installs a module; returns its `plugin.list` entry. The desktop app and `vectorcraft-cli` keep it in the `Plug-ins` folder next to the preferences, so it is installed again after a restart (#2541). A [heavy filter](#heavy-filters) installs only with `allowHeavy: true`, once the user agreed. |
| `plugin.inspect` | as `plugin.install`: `{"path"}` or `{"dataBase64", "name"?}` | Validates a module without installing it; returns the `plugin.list` entry it would have. |
| `plugin.remove` | `{"id"}` | Uninstalls, and deletes it from the `Plug-ins` folder. |
| `plugin.reload` | `{"path"?: "folder"}` (default: the preference folder) | Installs every `*.wasm` in a folder; a bad module is reported and skipped, and so is a heavy filter (nobody was asked). |

Live effects are applied like any effect: `effect.apply {"effect": "plugin.<id>", "params": {…}}`, edited with
`effect.setParams`, listed by `effect.list` (menu `Effect › Plug-ins`) and baked by Object › Expand Appearance.

An exporter adds a write-only format, `plugin.<id>`, which `document.formats` lists with its `plugin` id.
`document.export {"format": "plugin.<id>", "params"?: {…}, "path"?}` writes it, and so does a `path` ending in one of
its extensions that no built-in format has; `selectedOnly` hands it the selection, as for the built-in formats.

In the app, installed filters appear under **Object › Plug-ins**, next to **Install Plug-in…** and **Reload
Plug-ins**; live effects under **Effect › Plug-ins** and in the Appearance panel's effect menu. A plug-in with
parameters gets a dialog generated from its schema (numbers, whole numbers, checkboxes, dropdowns, text and lists
of numbers, labelled, explained and sorted into sections as its manifest says) with a live preview; without
parameters it runs at once. Parameters too many for the window's height scroll inside the dialog, which keeps its
heading and buttons in view. Exporters are formats of **File › Export › Export As**, where Use
Artboards is greyed out (the plug-in writes the whole document); one with parameters asks for them in a dialog of the
same kind once the file is picked, and its Export button writes the file. **File › Open** of a `.wasm` file installs
a plug-in too (on the web this is how plug-ins get in). A heavy filter asks before it is installed, and runs in the
background ([below](#heavy-filters)).

**Preference folder.** Edit › Preferences › Plug-ins & Scratch Disks › *Additional Plug-ins Folder*: when set, every
`*.wasm` in that folder (not recursive) is installed at startup and whenever the preference changes (desktop builds;
the web build installs from bytes).

Plug-ins are installed **per process**, not per document. Documents store a live effect as an ordinary effect record
(`{"id": "plugin.<id>", "params": {…}}`): while the plug-in is installed it is drawn, exported and expanded; without it
the object is drawn as if the effect weren't there, and the record is kept for when the plug-in comes back.

## The sandbox

The host is [`wasmi`](https://huve.tcti.cn/wenzhang/forecast-60448214.html), a pure-Rust WebAssembly interpreter
(MIT OR Apache-2.0). It builds for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` too, so plug-ins also run in the web build. Limits
(`vectorcraft_plugins::Limits`, defaults):

| Limit | Default | On violation |
|---|---|---|
| Host imports | none: no WASI, file system, network, clock or randomness | module rejected at install |
| Module size | 32 MiB | rejected |
| Linear memory | 512 MiB per instance (input and parameters: at most half) | `memory.grow` returns -1; oversized input or initial memory fails |
| Output | 64 MiB of JSON | `Limit("output size")` |
| Instructions (fuel) | 50 M per call + 4,000 per input byte for `vc_run`; a [heavy filter](#heavy-filters) 1 G + 4,000 per byte; an export 10 G + 4,000 per byte | `Limit("instruction budget")` |
| Wall clock | 60 s per filter run, 5 s per live-effect run, 300 s per heavy filter run or export (desktop; checked every 20 M instructions) | `Limit("time budget")` |
| Call depth | 1,024 frames | trap |
| Module shape | wasmi's strict limits (≤ 10,000 functions, 1 memory, …) | rejected |

An export runs where the export runs: with Background Export on, on the export's worker, whose Cancel stops the
plug-in between two of those 20 M-instruction slices; nothing is written then.

### Heavy filters

Some filters do heavy but legitimate work, such as routing a plotter's pen, packing shapes onto a sheet or running a
simulation, which a minute and 50 M instructions don't cover. Such a filter declares `"budget": "heavy"` in its
manifest (only a filter may: a live effect runs whenever the document is drawn, and an exporter has an export's
budget). Each of its runs gets 1 G instructions (20 times a light run's) plus the 4,000 per input byte, and 300 s
(`vectorcraft_plugins::{HEAVY_FUEL, HEAVY_WALL_TIME_MS}`). Its output can't add to the budget: the host learns how
much there is only once the run has ended.

- **Installing asks first.** Install Plug-in… and File › Open show what the filter asks for, and install it once the
  user clicks OK; `plugin.install` refuses it without `allowHeavy: true`, which an agent passes once the user agreed
  (`plugin.inspect` tells it beforehand). A filter kept in the `Plug-ins` folder was agreed to and is installed again
  at startup. The Additional Plug-ins Folder skips heavy filters with a note in its report, since loading a folder
  asks nobody.
- **It runs in the background.** Its dialog has no Preview. OK (or the menu item, without parameters) runs it on a
  thread of its own while editing goes on, shown in the status bar and, after a moment, in a progress window with
  Cancel (also Esc) and Continue in Background (`plugin.cancelRuns`, `plugin.hideRuns`). When it is done its result is
  applied as `plugin.run` with the same parameters and objects, as one undo step, unless the document or the plug-in
  changed meanwhile: then nothing changes, and the status bar says to run it again. On the web, which has no threads,
  it runs at once; the instruction budget alone bounds it there.
- `plugin.run` itself runs a heavy filter where it is called, as it runs any filter: an MCP client waits for it, and
  its `notifications/cancelled` stops it.

Every run gets a **fresh instance**, so no state survives between calls. Traps, exhausted budgets, malformed
modules, bad manifests, out-of-range pointers, negative return codes and invalid output all become errors, and the
document is left untouched: a filter's output is checked completely before one edit applies it. A live effect that
fails draws the object's geometry unchanged; `plugin.info` reports why (`lastError`).

wasmi is built with its *portable* (loop) dispatcher: the default tail-call dispatcher relies on LLVM
sibling-call optimisation, and when that doesn't happen a long-running module overflows the host stack, which aborts
the process instead of returning an error.

wasmi compiles each function when it is first called, and the instruction budget doesn't pay for that, so a run
takes as many instructions the first time as the next. Charged to the run, as wasmi charges by default, compiling
could fail it: when the 20 M-instruction slice the run was in ran out while a function compiled, wasmi ended the run
with an error rather than a pause the host resumes, and the run stopped with most of its budget left.

Drawing evaluates effects often, so live-effect results are cached by plug-in installation, parameters and input
geometry: a plug-in runs again only when one of them changes.

## ABI v1

A plug-in is a core WebAssembly module (MVP + the usual post-MVP features: bulk memory, sign extension, multi-value,
saturating conversions; no SIMD, no memory64) with **no imports** and these exports. Integers are `i32` unless noted;
pointers are offsets into the module's memory.

| Export | Signature | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `memory` | memory | The module's linear memory. |
| `vc_abi_version` | `() -> i32` | Must return `1`. |
| `vc_manifest` | `() -> i64` | `(len << 32) \| ptr` of the UTF-8 manifest JSON (≤ 64 KiB). |
| `vc_alloc` | `(size) -> ptr` | A block of `size` bytes the host may write, or `0` on failure. Never freed: each run gets a fresh instance. |
| `vc_run` | `(input, input_len, params, params_len) -> i64` | Runs the plug-in on the input JSON with the parameters JSON; returns `(len << 32) \| ptr` of the output JSON, or a negative error code. |

### Manifest

```json
{
  "id": "org.example.tidy",
  "name": "Tidy Paths",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "kind": "filter",
  "author": "Example",
  "description": "What it does.",
  "params": {
    "amount": {"type": "number", "min": 0, "max": 100, "default": 50, "unit": "%"},
    "steps":  {"type": "int", "min": 1, "max": 16, "default": 4, "label": "Steps per curve"},
    "closed": {"type": "bool", "default": false},
    "mode":   {"type": "choice", "options": ["soft", "hard"], "default": "soft",
               "help": "Soft keeps the corners round; hard keeps them sharp."}
  }
}
```

- `id`: 1–64 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -` (reverse-DNS recommended). Installing a module with the same id
  replaces the old one. A live effect's effect id is `plugin.<id>`.
- `name`: the menu label, or an exporter's format name in Export As (1–64 printable characters). `kind`: `"filter"`
  (object filter), `"effect"` (live effect) or `"exporter"`. Exporters came after the first ABI v1 hosts, which refuse
  the kind when the plug-in is installed.
- `budget` (filters only): `"light"` (the default) or `"heavy"`, for work that takes minutes ([heavy
  filters](#heavy-filters)). Hosts from before it ignore the key, so there the filter gets a light run's budget.
- `extensions` (exporters only, and required): 1–8 file extensions, lower-case letters and digits without the dot
  (`["plt"]`); the first is the one Export As gives the file. A built-in format keeps an extension both list (`svg`):
  `document.export` then writes the exporter's format only when asked for by its format id.
- `params`: in dialog order. Names are `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, not starting with `_`, and not `id`, `ids`, `params` or
  `preview`. The host validates the user's values before calling: missing values take the default, numbers are
  clamped to `min..max` (ints rounded), a wrong type or an unknown choice is an error. Numeric defaults
  are also clamped to their range, including the implicit zero default of an `int` parameter. Besides `number`,
  `int`, `bool` and `choice` there are `string` (`{"type": "string", "default": "", "maxLength": 256}`: a text field;
  longer text is cut to `maxLength`, at most 4,096 characters) and `numberList` (`{"type": "numberList", "min": 0,
  "max": 360, "default": [45, 135], "minItems": 1, "maxItems": 16}`: numbers typed separated by commas or spaces,
  each clamped to `min..max`; a list of too few or too many is an error, and `maxItems` is at most 256). A plug-in
  declares up to 256 parameters, at most 64 of them outside groups.

Each parameter may also say how dialogs show it. Hosts from before these keys ignore them, so a plug-in that
declares them still installs there:

| Key | What the dialog does with it |
|---|---|
| `label` | Labels the field (1–64 characters). Without one, the label is the name spaced out (`rowSpacing` → Row Spacing). |
| `unit` | Shows the unit the value is in after it (1–16 characters, such as `mm` or `°`). Nothing is converted: the plug-in gets the number as typed. |
| `group` | Puts the parameter in a section that folds (1–64 characters). Parameters outside any group come first, then each group in the order it first appears. |
| `help` | Shows what the parameter does when the pointer rests on its label (1–1,000 characters; line breaks allowed). |
| `helpUrl` | Opens this `https://` page (at most 512 bytes) from a button after the field. |
| `visibleWhen` | `{"pattern": ["lines", "crosshatch"], "outline": [true]}` shows the parameter only while each parameter it names (a checkbox or a choice declared before it) has one of the values listed and is shown itself. |

A hidden parameter still goes to the plug-in with its value: what the dialog showed never changes a run. The
filter, live-effect and exporter dialogs use all of these keys. The Appearance panel's editor of a plug-in effect's
parameters uses `label`, `unit`, `help` and `visibleWhen`, and lists the parameters without sections or help buttons.

### Input

`input` is UTF-8 JSON: `{"objects": [...]}`. An object filter gets the selected paths and compound paths in paint
order (bottom first): the selected ones and those inside selected groups and layers; hidden, locked, guide and clipping
paths are left out, and so are other kinds of object (type, images, symbols, live blends…), which a filter never
touches. With nothing selected the list is empty (a generator then adds its own objects). A live effect gets one
object: its geometry (`type`, `path`, `fillRule`, `bounds`) and its `fills` and `strokes`, as a filter gets them (hosts
from before these give geometry only). The paints are read only: an effect may draw as wide as a stroke or use a
fill's colour to decide its shape, but it changes only the geometry.

An **exporter** gets something else: the document as a native `.vectorcraft` file's JSON, as `document.save` writes it
but without indentation (the format is documented in [`crates/format/src/lib.rs`](../crates/format/src/lib.rs)). That is every layer, object,
appearance and effect record, artboard, swatch and symbol, so an exporter reads whatever the document holds; it checks
`version`, since a later host may write a newer one. Images of 8 KiB or more are listed in `images` with their MIME
type and `blob` but without their data, which follows the JSON in a saved file; smaller ones keep their base64 `data`.

```json
{"objects": [
  {"id": 12, "type": "path", "name": "Leaf",
   "path": {"subpaths": [{"closed": true, "anchors": [
     {"p": [10, 10]},
     {"p": [60, 10], "in": [45, 0], "out": [75, 20], "kind": "Smooth"},
     {"p": [35, 60]}]}]},
   "fillRule": "nonzero",
   "fills": [{"type": "solid", "color": {"model": "rgb", "r": 0.9, "g": 0.2, "b": 0.1}}],
   "strokes": [{"paint": {"type": "gradient", "gradient": {"kind": "Linear", "stops": [
       {"offset": 0, "color": {"model": "gray", "k": 0}},
       {"offset": 1, "color": {"model": "cmyk", "c": 0, "m": 0.5, "y": 1, "k": 0}}]}, "angle": 0},
     "width": 2, "join": "round", "cap": "butt", "miterLimit": 10}],
   "effects": [{"id": "distort.roughen", "params": {"detail": 10, "points": "smooth", "relative": true, "seed": 0,
     "size": 5}, "visible": true}],
   "opacity": 1,
   "bounds": [10, 0, 75, 60]}
]}
```

- `type`: `"path"` or `"compound"` (a compound path: `path` holds its members' subpaths, painted as one).
- `path`: VectorCraft's own path form. Each subpath is a run of anchors; `p` is the anchor, `in` / `out` its handles
  (absent: no handle), `kind` `"Smooth"` when the handles stay collinear. Coordinates are points, y down.
- `fills`, `strokes`: the object's fills and strokes in paint order (bottom first); `null` is no paint. A stroke has its
  `paint`, `width` in points, `join` (`"miter"`, `"round"` or `"bevel"`), `cap` (`"butt"`, `"round"` or `"square"`)
  and `miterLimit`. Paints use the
  native file format's form: `{"type": "solid", "color", "swatch"?, "tint"?}`, `{"type": "gradient", "gradient":
  {"kind": "Linear"|"Radial"|"Freeform", "stops": [{offset, color, opacity, midpoint}], "dither"?, "method"?: "Perceptual"}, "geom"?, "angle",
  "freeform"?}`, `{"type": "pattern", "pattern", "xf"?}`. Colours are `{"model": "rgb", r, g, b}`, `{"model": "cmyk",
  c, m, y, k}`, `{"model": "gray", k}` (ink: 0 white, 1 black) or `{"model": "lab", l, a, b}`; components 0–1 except
  Lab's.
- `effects` (filters): the object's own effects in order, as its effect records: `id` (as `effect.list` lists it, or
  `plugin.<id>` for a live-effect plug-in), `params` and `visible`. Its fills' and strokes' own effects aren't listed.
- `bounds`: `[x0, y0, x1, y1]`, the geometric bounds (read only).

### Parameters

`params` points at `params_len` bytes of UTF-8 JSON: the validated parameters, plus `_context`:

```json
{"amount": 50, "mode": "soft",
 "_context": {"mode": "filter", "bounds": [10, 0, 75, 60], "artboard": [0, 0, 612, 792], "documentData": {"pens": 4}}}
```

`mode` is `"filter"`, `"effect"` or `"export"`; `bounds` the selection's geometric bounds (a live effect: the reference
box of the effect, the object's bounds or those of the previous effect's result); `artboard` (filters) the artboard
under the selection's centre, else the first; `documentData` (filters) what the plug-in last kept with the document
(`null` until it keeps something; see Output). A live effect's `item` says where it sits: `"object"` (one of the
object's effects), or `{"fill": i}` / `{"stroke": i}` (in the own effects of the object's `i`th fill or stroke,
counted from the bottom as in `fills` and `strokes`). An export's `_context` is `{"mode": "export", "extension": "plt",
"name": "Poster"}` instead: the extension of the file being written (one the exporter lists) and its name without the
extension (the document's name when the export is not given a path), which some formats keep in their header.

### Output

The output is UTF-8 JSON in the input's shape: `{"objects": [...]}`. To decline with a message for the user, return
`{"error": "Select two paths."}`.

For an **object filter**, the output is the new state of the input objects:

- An object with the `id` of an input object updates it; keys it leaves out keep their value (`{"id": 12}` keeps the
  object as it is). `fills` and `strokes` set the object's fills and strokes in order: extra entries add fills (above
  the last one) or strokes, missing ones are removed; each stroke keeps its weight, join, cap and miter limit unless
  `width`, `join`, `cap` or `miterLimit` are given (a new one: 1 pt, miter join, butt cap, miter limit 10).
- `effects` replaces the object's own effects, in order: each `{id, params?, visible?}`. A record the object already had
  stays as it is; a new one is admitted as `effect.apply` admits it: an effect `effect.list` lists or an installed
  live-effect plug-in, with parameters it takes (filled in to their defaults; a plug-in's checked against its
  manifest), at most one 3D effect (its fills' and strokes' own effects counted), which must fit the object, and a
  Glass `textureImage` as Glass stores it (base64 of a PNG: a plug-in can't have the host read a file). A tool can
  then set up objects for a live effect in one step.
- An object without an `id` is new and needs a `path`. It goes just above the object listed before it, or, listed
  before any input object, just below the first one listed after it. New objects take a path's defaults: no fills or
  strokes, full opacity.
- Input objects missing from the output are deleted. The order of the input objects themselves doesn't change.
- `type` turns a path into a compound path (one member per subpath) or back; `name: ""` clears the name.
- A `path` returned as it was keeps a live shape live (a rectangle keeps its corner widgets); a changed one makes it a
  plain path.

The host validates everything before the document changes: coordinates must be finite and within ±4,000,000 pt, at
most 100,000 objects and 4,000,000 anchors, 256 fills, strokes or gradient stops; colours, opacities and offsets are
clamped into range, stroke weights to 0–1,000 pt and miter limits to 1–500; a pattern must exist in the document. A
paint returned unchanged keeps its swatch link; any other paint is unlinked. One refused effect record refuses the
whole output.

A filter's output may also hold `documentData`: any JSON of at most 1 MiB, which replaces what the plug-in keeps with
the document (`null` removes it), in the same undo step as its objects. Settings that belong to the whole document
rather than to one object go there, such as the pens a plotter holds. A filter reads and writes only its own data. It
is the document's foreign data, as the perspective grid is: the native file keeps it in `document.unknown.pluginData`
under the plug-in's id, and hosts from before `documentData` keep it when they save. An exporter is given the whole
document, so it can read what every plug-in keeps there, not only its own. A live effect isn't given it: its geometry
is worked out from the object alone.

For a **live effect**, the geometry of every returned object's `path` (their subpaths, in order) replaces the
object's; the rest is ignored (the object keeps its own appearance). An empty list removes the geometry.

An **exporter** returns `{"dataBase64": "…", "warnings"?: ["…"]}`: the file, in base64, which the host writes as it
is, and what the export left out or changed, for the user (at most 100 warnings of at most 500 characters each, shown
with the export's own). A decline (`{"error": …}`), a missing `dataBase64` or data that isn't base64 writes nothing.

## Writing a plug-in in Rust

[`crates/plugins/example`](../crates/plugins/example) is a complete object filter, **Desaturate**: it moves every
colour of the selection towards grey, in each colour's own model, using `serde_json` (no imports, no WASI). Build it
with:

```sh
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
crates/plugins/example/build.sh      # cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
```

The script also refreshes `crates/plugins/tests/fixtures/desaturate.wasm`, the test fixture built from that source.
The crate is not a workspace member. Any language that targets core WebAssembly works (C, Zig, AssemblyScript,
WAT…), as long as the module has no imports: in Rust, `std` on `wasm32-unknown-unknown` is fine as long as it never
touches WASI. `vectorcraft_plugins::wat::module` is the skeleton of a plug-in in WebAssembly text, which the tests
build their plug-ins from; `wat::echo_exporter` is an exporter whose file is its input or its parameters (with a
base64 encoder written out in WebAssembly text), which the tests read back what the host hands a plug-in with, and
`wat::when_given` a plug-in whose output depends on whether its input or parameters hold a given text, which shows in a
live effect's geometry.

## Performance

The interpreter costs roughly 10–100× native speed per instruction. Filters handle a selection in one call, so a
plug-in that parses and writes JSON with `serde_json` takes milliseconds for hundreds of paths. Live effects run once
per change of their input, parameters or paints (results are cached), not per frame.

## Not in v1

- Tool plug-ins (pointer events on the canvas, a guide line or rectangle, geometry back), panel plug-ins, host
  callbacks (a plug-in reporting progress or asking whether it was cancelled), importers (plug-in formats that open
  files).
- Live effects that change paint (they reshape geometry; an object filter recolours), and filters on type, images or
  symbols.
- Apply Last Effect and Last Effect work for plug-in effects; there is no "last filter" for object filters yet.

### Print a large poster across multiple pages

# Print a large poster across multiple pages

## Overview

Use tiled printing to spread a large poster, sign or sewing pattern across several sheets of A4,
Letter or other paper. VectorCraft divides the drawing into numbered tiles at the scale you choose.
Overlap repeats part of the drawing on adjacent sheets to help you align them after printing.

## Print a poster on multiple sheets

1. Open your drawing in VectorCraft. For a full-size pattern, check that the drawing has the intended
   dimensions before printing.
2. Choose **File → Print…** to open VectorCraft's **Print** dialog. In **Printer**, select your printer
   or **PDF File** to save the tiled job as a PDF.
3. In **General**, under **Artboards**, choose **All** or **Range:** to select the artboards to print.
   For example, use **Range:** `1` for the first artboard. Choose **Ignore Artboards (all the art as
   one page)** only if you want to tile the bounds of all the artwork instead of individual artboards.
4. Under **Media**, set **Size** to the paper loaded in the printer, such as **A4**, **Letter** or a Japanese paper (**B5 (JIS)**, **Japanese Postcard**, **Japanese Envelope #3**).
   Choose **Custom** to enter **Width** and **Height**. **Auto-Rotate (turn the paper to each artboard)**
   is on by default; turn it off to choose a fixed **Orientation**, such as **Portrait** or **Landscape**.
5. In **Advanced**, set **Unprintable margin** to allow for the edges your printer cannot print.
   VectorCraft uses one value for all four edges; use a value that covers the printer's largest
   required margin. The default is zero, and VectorCraft does not read this value from the printer.
6. Return to **General**. Under **Options**, set **Scaling** to **Tile Imageable Areas** or
   **Tile Full Pages** (see [Choose a tiling mode](#choose-a-tiling-mode)). Set **Scale**, both **W**
   and **H**, to `100%` to keep the drawing's size. Use the same percentage in both fields to keep
   its proportions; larger percentages enlarge the drawing and can require more sheets.
7. Set **Overlap** to repeat a strip along adjoining tiles. For example, `10 mm` gives room for
   alignment. Length fields accept units such as `mm` and `in`. Overlap must be less than half
   the smaller tile dimension; increasing it can increase the sheet count.
8. Leave **Tile Range** empty initially. Use the **Previous page** and **Next page** arrows beneath
   the preview to inspect each sheet. The label identifies its artboard and tile; the preview also
   shows the paper size and scale. Check **Summary** for warnings or invalid settings.
9. Keep **Tile Range** empty to print every tile, or enter a range such as `1-3, 5` to print a subset.
   Check the preview again after changing the range.
10. Click **Print**. With a printer selected, VectorCraft sends the laid-out job to the system's print
    service. With **PDF File** selected, it asks where to save the PDF, with one page per printed
    tile for each copy in composite output. **Done** keeps the print settings with the document
    without printing; save the document to retain them for next time.

The tiling controls belong to VectorCraft's **Print** dialog on Windows, macOS and Linux.
**Setup…**, beside **Printer**, opens the system's printer settings, whose interface varies by
platform. Set tiling in VectorCraft's **Scaling** list. Keep the printer's paper settings consistent
with **Media**. In the web app, printing goes through the browser's print dialog; **PDF File**
downloads the PDF.

For a paper proof, select **PDF File** and click **Print**, then open the saved PDF to inspect its
pages before sending it to a printer. When printing that PDF, keep its page size and scale rather
than applying another fit-to-page reduction. For a sewing pattern, measure a known length on a
printed sheet before printing the full job.

## Choose a tiling mode

| Scaling | How it divides the drawing | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Tile Full Pages** | Each tile uses the full paper width and height. Adjacent tiles advance by that size minus **Overlap**. | Use when you need a grid based on whole sheets, such as with a printer that supports the required borderless paper setting. On a printer with unprintable edges, artwork near tile edges can be lost unless sufficient overlap covers those gaps. |
| **Tile Imageable Areas** | Each tile uses the paper area inside **Unprintable margin**. Adjacent tiles advance by that smaller size minus **Overlap**. | Use for printers with unprintable edges. Set the margin in **Advanced** so the tiles account for those edges; this can require more sheets than full-page tiling. |

With **Unprintable margin** set to zero, the two modes use the same tile dimensions. Neither mode
makes a printer capable of borderless printing. **Fit to Page** scales an artboard onto a single
sheet; choose a tile mode to keep a large drawing spread across sheets.

## Check the layout on the canvas

1. Set up tiling in **File → Print…**, then click **Done** to keep the settings.
2. Choose **View → Show Print Tiling**. The canvas shows each sheet's paper edge and a dashed,
   numbered imageable area. Tiles excluded by **Tile Range** appear dimmer. The overlay uses the
   saved print settings; it does not print anything.
3. Select the **Print Tiling Tool**. In the default toolbar, press and hold the **Hand Tool** button
   in the **Navigate** group to open its tool list, then choose **Print Tiling Tool**. The tool also
   shows the overlay while it is active.
4. Drag on the canvas to position the grid. The pointer places the top-left corner of a page's
   imageable area and snaps near artboard edges. Tiles extend left and up as needed to cover the
   drawing, so that page may not be tile 1 after the move. Reopen **File → Print…** to check the
   resulting pages and tile numbers. Dragging the dialog's preview does not reposition tiled pages.

To restore the default grid position, double-click on the canvas with **Print Tiling Tool** active,
or double-click the tool's toolbar button. Alternatively, reopen **File → Print…** and click
**Reset** beneath **Placement** when the dialog says **The Print Tiling tool placed the pages.**
Click **Done** to keep that change. **View → Hide Print Tiling** hides the overlay after switching
to another tool.

## Print only selected tiles

**Tile Range** uses numbers starting at 1, across each row from left to right, then down.
For a grid with three columns and two rows, the first row is `1, 2, 3` and the second is `4, 5, 6`.
Enter `2, 5` to print the middle column, or `1-3, 5` to print the first row and tile 5.
Leave the field empty to print all tiles.

**Range:** under **Artboards** selects drawings; **Tile Range** selects sheets within each chosen
drawing. Tile numbering restarts for each artboard, and the same tile range applies to each one.
To reprint one damaged sheet of one artboard, select that artboard with **Range:** and its tile
with **Tile Range**. A tile number must exist on every selected artboard. Changing paper, scale,
margin, overlap or grid position can change the grid and its numbering; check again before reprinting.

## Assemble the printed sheets

Lay out the sheets in tile order. Align repeated artwork in the overlap, trim unprinted edges as
needed, and tape or glue the sheets together. Print a pair of adjacent tiles first to check the
scale, margins and overlap before committing to a large job.

## Troubleshooting

- **The preview shows only one page.** It displays one sheet at a time. Use the arrows and check
  the count beneath it. If the count is one, check **Tile Range**, the chosen artboards, paper size
  and scale: the drawing may fit on one tile.
- **The image shrinks to one sheet.** Change **Scaling** from **Fit to Page** to a tile mode and
  check both scale percentages. Also check for another fit-to-page setting when printing a saved PDF.
- **Artwork is missing along sheet edges.** Check the printer's unprintable margins. Use
  **Tile Imageable Areas** with a suitable **Advanced → Unprintable margin**, or allow enough
  overlap in full-page tiling to cover the missing edges. Check that the physical paper matches
  **Media**; a zero margin does not remove a printer's hardware limits.
- **No tiling boundaries appear on the canvas.** Keep the settings with **Done**, then enable
  **View → Show Print Tiling** or select **Print Tiling Tool**. If the settings are invalid, the
  overlay has no pages to draw; reopen **Print** and check **Summary**.
- **The job has the wrong number of pages.** Check **Artboards**, **Tile Range**, **Copies** and
  **Skip Blank Artboards**. Paper size, orientation, scale, margins and overlap affect the grid.
  Under **Output**, **Mode → Separations** produces a page per enabled ink; use **Composite** for
  an ordinary poster. The dialog preview shows one copy; the saved PDF includes all copies.

## Related documentation

- [Printing and PDF file output](mcp.md#printing) — command reference.
- [Print tiling](mcp.md#print-tiling) — overlay and positioning command reference.
- [Print settings](mcp.md#print) — paper, scaling and output settings reference.
